text: A Business Rule is a server-side script that runs automatically whenever a record on a specified table is inserted, updated, deleted, or queried. It's the most powerful, and most dangerous, automation mechanism on the whole platform, and this lesson is about understanding exactly why.

Every Business Rule you'll ever write is stored as a row on the sys script table. The script body receives the record being processed automatically, as a variable called current. Nobody opens a menu and clicks run. You save a record, and somewhere on the server this script quietly executes.

A Business Rule's trigger is defined by checkboxes on the rule record: insert, update, delete, and query. The same script can be configured to fire on any combination. One set to run on insert only fires for brand-new records. One set to run on update fires every single time an existing record is saved again.

Here's what makes Business Rules fundamentally different from the UI Policies and Data Policies you already know. Those run in the browser, or close to the database, scoped to one form. A Business Rule runs on the application server, inside the same transaction as the database write, with full access to any table in the instance — not just the one the user is looking at.

A UI Policy can hide a field. A Business Rule can rewrite data anywhere in your instance, on every single save, silently, using access the logged-in user might not even have themselves. That reach is exactly what makes it powerful. It's also exactly what makes it dangerous — a careless rule doesn't produce one wrong answer, it produces that wrong answer thousands of times a day, on every matching record.

Treat every Business Rule as code running in production the moment you activate it, because that's literally what it is. Next, we'll break down the four real timing types — before, after, async, and display — and why each one exists for a completely different reason.
